prompt.context: Your client is EdCo, an education publishing company. They sell both software and textbooks, and within those two categories they sell both general subject area materials and materials targeted at intervention (materials aimed at students who are falling behind in a subject area, intended to help them catch up). Growth, both on a revenue and profit basis, has been slowing. EdCo has retained us to help them find ways to revive growth.
prompt.question: How should EdCo revive its growth? Where should it focus, and how should it go about growing in that area?

clarifying_info.q: What is the revenue breakdown by segment?
What is the profit breakdown by segment?
What is the growth outlook for the general subject area segment?
clarifying_info.a: Very few growth opportunities. General subject area materials, both software and textbooks, are sold on long-term contracts with standard replacement cycles, and the market is saturated. The entire industry is suffering due to school district funding cutbacks.

clarifying_info.q: What is the growth outlook for the intervention segment?
clarifying_info.a: EdCo believes this is a severely underserved market. Education experts and activists overwhelmingly agree. Many students in need of specialized content to help them catch up are not being effectively reached.

clarifying_info.q: What is the growth outlook for software vs. textbooks?
clarifying_info.a: Research indicates growth going forward will continue to be on the software side, particularly with content that needs to be more customized to the individual student.

The textbook business is a legacy business — EdCo is good at it but cannot differentiate. On software, EdCo has leading design and programming departments and believes it has an edge. On intervention, EdCo is considered a leader — studies show its software is more effective at raising student achievement than competitors.

clarifying_info.q: How does the intervention software revenue model work?
clarifying_info.a: The software is sold on a license basis: a school buys, for example, 50 licenses for the right and ability to have 50 students using the software in a given school year. The entire cost is paid up-front, and periodic minor updates are provided going forward. A new student can use the same license each new school year.

exhibits.title: Intervention software market shares
exhibits.shows: A table of market share percentages for the intervention software market, broken down by grade band (K-5 at 60% of the market, 6-12 at 40% of the market) for Competitor A, Competitor B, and the Client.

exhibits.title: Customer data — school districts
exhibits.shows: A table of school district data broken down by district size (Small, Medium, Large), showing number of districts, percentage of total remedial student population, and EdCo's district penetration (number of districts EdCo is present in). Total remedial student population is 2,000,000.

framework: Segment analysis: evaluate the four segments (subject area textbooks, subject area software, intervention textbooks, intervention software) on profitability, market growth, and competitive position to identify where to focus
Market position: assess EdCo's competitive standing and market share in the chosen focus segment, including granular breakdowns (e.g., by grade band)
Customer targeting: analyze customer data to identify the most attractive and underserved customer segment to prioritize sales efforts
Barriers to adoption: identify what prevents customers from purchasing or expanding use of the product and how those barriers can be overcome
Recommendation: synthesize findings into a prioritized growth action plan with risks and next steps

questions.prompt: Part 1: Which of EdCo's four segments (subject area textbooks, subject area software, intervention textbooks, intervention software) should be the focus for growth?
questions.guidance: Candidate should combine revenue breakdown (65% software / 35% textbooks; 60% intervention / 40% subject area), profit breakdown (75% software / 25% textbooks; 80% intervention / 20% subject area), market outlook (general subject area saturated and declining due to funding cuts; intervention severely underserved and growing), and core competencies (software and intervention are EdCo strengths; textbooks are legacy with no differentiation) to conclude that intervention software is the clear focus: it is the biggest segment, carries the highest margins, operates in a growing and underserved market, and aligns with EdCo's competitive advantage.

questions.prompt: Part 2: Using Exhibit 1, calculate EdCo's overall market share, the market shares of its top 2 competitors, and the remaining fragmented market share in the intervention software segment.
questions.guidance: Candidate should set total market = 100, split K-5 = 60 and 6-12 = 40, then calculate weighted market shares. A strong candidate will also draw conclusions about EdCo's strengths and weaknesses by grade band (dominant in 6-12, weak in K-5) and hypothesize what might explain the K-5 gap (weaker sales relationships, weaker product, competitor pricing deals in K-5).

math.setup: Set total market = 100. K-5 segment = 60, 6-12 segment = 40. Multiply each player's grade-band share by the segment size and sum.
math.answer: EdCo: 24% (market leader). Competitor B: 16%. Competitor A: 13%. Fragmented others: 47%. EdCo is dominant in 6-12 (45% share) but weak in K-5 (10% share).

questions.prompt: Part 3: Using Exhibit 2, calculate the number of unreached remedial students in each district size category. Which district segment should EdCo target first?
questions.guidance: A great candidate first proposes calculating unreached students and uses both the district-level penetration gap and a second-order insight about student-level penetration within districts where EdCo already has a relationship. Missing information: although EdCo may have a presence in a district, they are only reaching a fraction of students in those districts (large: 10%, medium: 40%, small: 75%). Candidates who do not notice this missing information can still perform well; they should not get flustered when probed. Conclusion: focus on large districts — largest unreached population and existing relationships with 90% of them already. Medium is second priority. Small districts unattractive due to small market and high customer acquisition cost.

math.setup: Total remedial students: 2M. Large districts: 50% of total = 1M. Medium: 40% = 800k. Small: 10% = 200k. EdCo district penetration: Large 900/1000, Medium 2000/4000, Small 1000/9000. Missing information revealed by interviewer: within districts where EdCo has a relationship, student-level penetration is Large 10%, Medium 40%, Small 75%.
steps: Large: districts not reached = 1000 - 900 = 100 → students unreached = 1,000,000 * (100/1000) = 100,000
Medium: districts not reached = 4000 - 2000 = 2000 → students unreached = 800,000 * (2000/4000) = 400,000
Small: districts not reached = 9000 - 1000 = 8000 → students unreached = 200,000 * (8000/9000) ≈ 178,000
--- With missing information (student-level penetration within EdCo districts) ---
Large: unreached in non-EdCo districts = 100,000; unreached in EdCo districts = 900,000 * (1 - 0.10) = 810,000; Total = 910,000
Medium: unreached in non-EdCo districts = 400,000; unreached in EdCo districts = 400,000 * (1 - 0.40) = 240,000; Total = 640,000
Small: unreached in non-EdCo districts ≈ 178,000; unreached in EdCo districts = 22,000 * (1 - 0.75) = 5,500; Total ≈ 183,500
math.answer: With full information — Large districts: ~910,000 unreached remedial students (largest opportunity, mostly existing relationships). Medium: ~640,000. Small: ~183,500 (least attractive — smallest market, low EdCo penetration, high acquisition cost per license).

questions.prompt: Part 4: What are the main barriers to adoption of EdCo's intervention software, and how can the company overcome them?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm multiple distinct categories of barriers (awareness, money/funding, technology infrastructure are key ones) and suggest concrete solutions for each. Interviewer should press with 'what else?' once or twice. Strong candidates go beyond listing to link solutions back to business model and EdCo's situation (e.g., subscription model also improves EdCo revenue stability).

brainstorming.prompt: What are the main barriers to adoption of EdCo's intervention software, and what are ways the company can attempt to bring down or overcome those barriers?

categories.name: Awareness
ideas: Schools or decision-makers may not know the product exists — survey stakeholders to measure awareness; develop a cost-effective marketing plan if awareness is low

Schools may not know EdCo's software produces superior student achievement outcomes vs. competitors — invest in raising awareness among key stakeholders including teachers, parents, journalists, and administrators who influence purchase decisions

categories.name: Money / Funding
ideas: License cost is paid entirely up-front, making it a large one-time expense — offer a subscription model for a more manageable payment structure (also gives EdCo a more stable revenue stream)
Volume discounts to incentivize districts to buy more licenses or consolidate to a single vendor (EdCo)
Versioning: create less functional but cheaper product tiers to reach schools with tight budgets
Packaging: bundle software with a textbook so schools can use different earmarked funding buckets (textbook budget + software budget) to make the purchase
Offer financing packages to spread the up-front cost

categories.name: Technology Infrastructure
ideas: If schools lack sufficient computer hardware, they cannot use the software — offer versions optimized for tablets (iPad/other), offline-capable versions, or versions designed for partial computer availability (e.g., rotating student groups)
Lobby non-market channels for schools to fund technology infrastructure investments

recommendation: EdCo should focus on the intervention software market because it is (1) a growing and severely underserved market, (2) the highest-margin segment, and (3) the area where EdCo has the clearest competitive advantage in product efficacy.

Within intervention software, EdCo should focus its sales efforts on large school districts: they represent the largest pool of unreached remedial students (~910,000), EdCo already has relationships with 90% of large districts, and these schools are more likely to have the funding to purchase the product.
risks: If EdCo does not identify and address the main barriers to adoption, sales efforts will be ineffective even in large districts.
Large districts have more bargaining power and the capacity to develop proprietary intervention software in-house.
It may be difficult to displace the intervention materials these large districts are currently using.
Other education software providers will continue to improve their offerings — EdCo must continue to invest in software development to maintain its product efficacy lead.
next_steps: Conduct deeper analysis of the large school district landscape to identify the most attractive specific targets.
Investigate the existence and strength of barriers to adoption (awareness, funding, technology) and design solutions to overcome them.
Develop a marketing and sales program targeting large districts, informed by the barriers-to-adoption analysis.
